In case anybody in the future has the same question, here
are the exact commands that I used:

# Create the ggplot object.  df is a dataframe
# containing a column named 'dates' that will be
# used for the x-axis.
plot <- ggplot (df, aes(x=dates));

# Set the text for the x-axis.  Note that since the data is
# of type Date, one must use scale_x_date.  For other data,
# one might use scale_x_discrete or scale_x_continuous.
plot <- plot + scale_x_date("Date");

# Set the text for the y-axis.
plot <-  plot + scale_y_continuous("Value");

# Set the text for the legend.
plot <- plot + scale_colour_discrete("Predictive model");

messages.body_plain:
Hi Owen,

Plot size is controlled by the dimensions of the graphic device you're
using, and in most cases R graphics (including ggplot) will rescale
themselves as well as they can to fit that.  If you are just viewing
output on screen, try resizing the plot window until you like how it
looks.  Then you can use the command par('din') to view the device
dimensions and use that as a guideline for setting the same dimensions
if/when you write a wrapper to send the plot to, say, a pdf file or
other saved graphics device.

Shelby

mtcars$cyl <- factor(mtcars$cyl)

library(ggplot2)

messages.subject_clean: customize y-axis label of a density plot
messages.body_plain:
Hi Philippe,

For this special case, you need to use the full form:  +
scale_y_continuous("Density")

The reason is because the y axis is a computed variable, so at the
time you create the plot, ggplot doesn't know whether it will be a
continuous or discrete variable and so doesn't add a default scale
(like it does for all the other variables).  xlab(), and labels() and
the xlab argument all working by modifying the existing scale, so they
don't work in this case because it doesn't exist.

Regards,

Hadley

messages.subject: Re: polar plots
messages.body_plain:
Hi Steve,

In principle, it's pretty easy, just forget about the polar
coordinates, and figure out how to get what you want in Cartesian
coordinates:

cxc <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_bar(width = 1, colour = "black")

cxc + geom_hline(yintercept = 5)
# OR
cxc + geom_segment(x = 0.5, xend = 3.5, y = 5, yend = 5)

Then you can just add the polar coordinates back on to turn the
horizontal line into a circle:

cxc + geom_hline(yintercept = 5) + coord_polar()
cxc + geom_segment(x = 0.5, xend = 3.5, y = 5, yend = 5) + coord_polar()

However, unfortunately bugs prevent either of these methods working in
the current version.  You can work around it as follows:

lines <- data.frame(x = c(0.5, 3.5),  y = c(4, 4))
cxc + geom_line(aes(x, y), data = lines)
cxc + geom_line(aes(x, y), data = lines) + coord_polar()

I've added the bugs to my to do list, so they should hopefully get
fixed in the not too distant future.

Regards,

Hadley

Hi Vikas,

You are better off controlling the grouping directly.  I think the
following should do what you want:

qplot(Year,CDR,data=b3,colour=Phase,geom=c("point","line"), group = 1)

By default, geoms are broken into groups by the combination of all
discrete variables used in the plot.  Here you don't want that break
up to occur, so override the default grouping to have only one group.

If you do want to get rid the legend, you can use the following option:
+ opts(drop = "legend")

Regards,

Hadley

messages.subject: ggsave and path on Mac
messages.body_plain:
I may be  crazy, but I think the path parameter on ggsave doesn't work
on Mac.

# path
this.dir <- "/Volumes/user/Documents/R Stuff/SRT/"
# path without trailing slash
this.dir <- "/Volumes/user/Documents/R Stuff/SRT"
# ggsave with path, works on windows and doesn't work on Mac
version 1:  ggsave(p, "fname.eps", path=this.dir)
# this works on both mac and windows
version 2:  ggsave(p, paste(this.dir, "fname.eps", sep=""))

Version 1 using the path does not work on Mac but does work on Windows
(I move regularly between the two systems). It's not a practical
problem; I just use version 2.  But I thought I'd note it.  Just in
case I tried a version leaving off the trailing / but that didn't make
a difference.  On mac, ggsave with just a file name saves the file
into the home directory.

By the way, I've found that using ".eps" gives me the best results
with Microsoft Word (at least on Windows).  My second best had been to
use the copy metafile in the Windows environment and then paste into
word.  But I had to screw around with sizes in Word and the result was
not always for the best.  With ".eps" I can specify the size in ggsave
and this works when I insert the picture file into my word document.
In other words, I disagree with the advice given in section 8.3 of the
book.

-- John Goldin

Ah ok.  One possibility is:

  opts(aspect.ratio=3/4)

legend.  You want a scale which is a combination of a continuous
colour gradient and a discrete colour (for missings) and there's no
built in scale that supports that.

messages.subject: Re: Adding a legend to facet_grid...
messages.body_plain:
I think I know what Adam means, and I think it's more a drawback of
how both lattice & ggplot2 label the facets while making the variable
determining the labels implicit.

For example, if your facet variable is called "Flower" with levels
"Rose" and "Daisy", the standard lattice/ggplot2 display of the facet
labels is to label the "Rose" facet as "Rose" and the "Daisy" facet as
"Daisy", leaving the fact that we're talking about the "Flower"
variable implicit.

To solve this I often re-label my factors to make the source factor
explicit to the graph reader:
levels(Flower) = c('Flower = Rose','Flower = Daisy')

An alternative is to specify in a figure caption the variable
determining the facets.

Hi there,

I am currently conducting a clinical study where I want to visualize
the effect of a medical treatment with different boxplots. I am using
ggplot + geom_boxplot for this task.

Unfortunately, there are some "bad" mavericks in my dataset that are
srewing up the drawing: the boxplot themselves are getting very very
tiny, because ggplot2 also wants to draw the far-outlying mavericks
onto the canvas. I tried to solve the problem by applying the xlim
operator, but the effect is that the mavericks are totally excluded
from the dataset, not only the drawing. This results in a totally
boxplot representation, as the median an the quartiles are affected by
this "cropping".

I wonder if there is a way to simply crop the drawing area, not the
values itself?

Any help is highly appreciated!!!

Thanks & all the best
Philipp
